messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol is a 39-year-old Latina woman who has spent most of her adult life working at a non-profit that serves immigrant families. Until last year, she had understood that work as part of who she was: being useful, being steady for other people, being connected to her neighborhood, her church, and the Spanish-speaking community she had always moved through with ease. The assault happened after an evening fundraising event, when she stayed late to help clean up. In a storage area behind the building, a man cornered her, threatened her with a weapon, and forced her to undress. What remains most vivid to her is not a clear sequence but a cluster of piercing images: the sight of the object in his hand, the exposure of her own body, and the certainty that violence could happen at any second. When she tries to tell the story, she stops and starts, saying she knows what happened but cannot find words for it; the pieces come out jumbled, and when they do, she is flooded with rage.

In the weeks afterward, those fragments began fastening themselves to moments in daily life. At work, a donor’s pocketknife left on a conference table, a news clip showing a street fight on the office television, even the vulnerable feeling of stepping out of the shower unclothed in her own apartment could make her whole body jolt. She did not experience these as reminders in any ordinary sense. The image of a weapon or any scene of violence seemed to tell her immediately that danger was present now. She startled violently at small noises, scanned her apartment at night, and could not take in reassurance from her husband when he told her the doors were locked and she was safe. Nights became the worst; darkness felt like exposure, and she stayed alert long after he had fallen asleep.

Just as painful was what these moments came to mean about her. Each time she recoiled from seeing violence on a screen or froze at the sight of an object that could be used as a weapon, Marisol felt humiliated by her own reaction. She had come to believe that somebody stronger, smarter, less foolish would never have gotten into that situation in the first place. Being triggered by nakedness was especially crushing to her, because it revived not only fear but a sense of degradation and weakness. The fact that ordinary images could undo her so quickly became, in her mind, evidence that she was a weak person.

That belief did not stay abstract. Marisol began to feel she no longer fit in the communities that had once anchored her. She stopped going to church events and pulled back from family gatherings, especially the lively evenings where people lingered late and talked over one another. She felt separate from other Latina women she had once felt proud to stand beside, certain they would see a woman who had failed to protect herself. The more she judged herself this way, the less she could believe in safety anywhere. Her husband’s reassurance landed as empty words because, to her mind, a weak person was never truly safe; if she had failed once, she could fail again. She became jumpier, more watchful at night, and increasingly convinced that danger was always close.

Her self-criticism also shaped the way she held the memory itself. When she tried to think about the assault, she would immediately begin comparing herself to an imagined other woman who would have acted differently. Then the memory would tangle. She could not put the moments in order, and her inability to describe what happened felt like further proof of inadequacy. At the same time, the broken, wordless quality of the memory made it feel less like something over and more like something unresolved and still capable of breaking into the present. When the images returned without sequence, rage surged through her body so abruptly that she would brace as if under threat again. Those furious, disorganized recollections left her even more certain that she was not coping the way she “should,” deepening the shame and self-blame she already carried.

Over months, the memory fragments, the shame, and the triggers tightened around each other. Because the event remained a set of vivid images rather than a story she could tell through, a glimpse of a weapon-shaped object or a scene of violence could instantly pull the assault close. Because she had come to see herself as weak and cut off from her people, she noticed these cues everywhere and experienced them as confirmations that the world was unsafe and that she was especially unprotected in it. At the non-profit, she now avoids staying late, refuses to go into storage rooms alone, and asks colleagues to handle community outreach events that run into the evening. She is frightened by how small her life has become, and by how far she feels from the woman she used to be. Marisol finally sought help after realizing she was dreading nightfall every day and no longer believed her husband when he said she was home and safe. What she wants most is to feel connected and recognizable to herself again, though what she fears most is that the assault revealed something permanently weak in her that she will never be able to undo.
